stages.title: Advanced grammar
explain: The subjunctive (le subjonctif) is used after verbs and expressions of necessity, wish, emotion and doubt: "il faut que", "je veux que", "je suis content que", "il est possible que". It is formed from the ils form of the present: "ils finissent" gives "que je finisse".

Some verbs are irregular: être (que je sois), avoir (que j'aie), aller (que j'aille), faire (que je fasse). Use the conditional for polite requests and hypotheses: "je voudrais", "tu pourrais". The plus-que-parfait (pluperfect) shows an earlier past action: "Il avait déjà mangé quand je suis arrivé."
sentences: It is necessary that we leave.

gq.q: Choose the correct form: Il faut que tu ___ ton travail.
gq.why: Il faut que triggers the subjunctive.

gq.q: Why does "Je pense qu'il vient" use the indicative while "Je ne pense pas qu'il vienne" uses the subjunctive?
gq.why: Affirmed opinion is certain; negated opinion expresses doubt.

panel.q: Which is the subjunctive of "être" for je?
What does the plus-que-parfait express?
o: An action before another past action
panel.why: It is the past of the past.

panel.q: Why does "après que" traditionally take the indicative while "avant que" takes the subjunctive?
o: After the event is a fact, before the event is not yet realised
panel.why: After describes something that has happened; avant que refers to an event still pending.

teach.model: The subjunctive is used after expressions of necessity, wish, emotion and doubt, like il faut que and je veux que. It is formed from the ils form of the present, with irregulars such as sois, aie and fasse.

stages.hook: Why does French say "Il faut que tu viennes" and not "Il faut que tu viens"?
stages.mnemonic: Wish, doubt, must, feel: the subjunctive is near the heart.

stages.title: Complex sentence patterns
explain: French "si" clauses follow patterns. Real possibility: si plus present, then future: "Si tu viens, je serai content." Unlikely or imagined: si plus imparfait, then conditional: "Si j'avais le temps, je voyagerais." Never use the future or conditional after "si" in the condition part.

The relative pronoun "dont" replaces "de + noun": "Le livre dont je parle." The passive uses être plus participle: "La lettre a été écrite par Marie", but French prefers "on" or a reflexive: "Ça se dit", "On parle français ici".
sentences: If I had time, I would travel.
Here is the book I am talking about.

gq.q: Choose the correct form: Si j'avais le temps, je ___
gq.why: Si plus imparfait takes the conditional.

gq.q: Why is "Si j'aurais le temps" incorrect?
o: Si is never followed by the conditional in the condition
gq.why: The conditional goes in the result clause only.

panel.q: Which sentence uses dont correctly?
o: Le film dont j'ai besoin est ici.
Le film que j'ai besoin est ici.
Le film qui j'ai besoin est ici.
Le film où j'ai besoin est ici.

panel.q: How does French often avoid the passive?
o: With on or a reflexive verb
panel.why: On parle français ici is a typical alternative.

panel.q: What does "même si" introduce?
o: A concession that is real or hypothetical

points.ask: How do I form imagined conditions?
How can I avoid the passive?

teach.model: Use si plus present with future for real conditions and si plus imparfait with conditional for imagined ones. Never put the conditional after si. Dont replaces de plus a noun.

stages.hook: What is the difference between "Si j'avais de l'argent, j'achèterais une maison" and "Si j'ai de l'argent, j'achèterai une maison"?
stages.mnemonic: Si + imparfait, conditionnel: dream; si + présent, futur: plan.

stages.title: Extended conversations
explain: To react: "Vraiment?", "Ah bon?", "C'est vrai?" To agree: "Tout à fait", "Je suis d'accord". To disagree politely: "Je ne suis pas tout à fait d'accord" or "Oui, mais...". To ask for clarification: "Qu'est-ce que vous voulez dire?"

Fillers like "en fait", "du coup", "alors" and "enfin" structure speech. Turn-taking is often overlapping in French conversation, which is normal and not rude. Keep the conversation flowing by asking follow-up questions: "Et alors?", "Pourquoi?"
items: Je ne suis pas tout à fait d'accord
sentences: I do not quite agree with you.

o: Je ne suis pas tout à fait d'accord
gq.why: The softening tout à fait makes disagreement polite.

o: To mark a consequence in informal speech
gq.why: It means so or as a result.

panel.q: A person overlaps your speech in a lively French discussion. What does it often mean?
panel.why: Overlapping is often a sign of interest.

panel.q: Which phrase asks for clarification formally?
Why does "Ah bon?" not mean "Oh good"?
o: It is a reaction meaning Really?
panel.why: Fixed expressions have their own meaning.

points.ask: How do I ask what they mean?

teach.model: In French conversation react with Ah bon or Vraiment. Agree with Tout à fait and disagree politely with Oui, mais. Ask for clarification with Qu'est-ce que vous voulez dire? Use fillers like en fait and du coup.

stages.hook: How do you keep a conversation going, disagree politely, and ask for clarification in French?
stages.mnemonic: Agree, add a "mais", ask back: three tools for any chat.

stages.title: Formal and informal registers
explain: French has three main registers: familier (casual), courant (standard) and soutenu (formal). "Voiture" is standard, "bagnole" is casual, "automobile" is formal. Friends say "tu"; strangers and elders get "vous".

Casual French drops ne, uses "on" for nous and shortens words: "J'sais pas", "On y va?" Formal French keeps ne, inverts the question and uses precise vocabulary: "Je ne sais pas", "Pouvez-vous m'indiquer?" Verlan reverses syllables: "meuf" comes from "femme".
sentences: I don't know where he is.

gq.q: Which sentence is the most formal?
o: Tu sais où est la gare?
gq.why: Conditional and inversion with vous are formal.

gq.q: Why does choosing the wrong register matter?
o: It can sound rude or oddly stiff
It changes the meaning of numbers

panel.q: What is verlan?
When is "on" used instead of "nous"?
panel.why: On is the common spoken form for we.

panel.q: A student writes "J'sais pas" in a formal essay. What is the problem?
o: A spoken register is used in a formal text
panel.why: Written formal French keeps ne and full forms.

teach.model: French has familier, courant and soutenu registers. Use tu with friends and vous with strangers, elders and groups. Casual speech drops ne and uses on; formal speech uses inversion and complete forms.

stages.hook: Why does a French teen say "T'as pas faim?" but a hotel receptionist says "Avez-vous faim?"
stages.mnemonic: Tu for friends, vous for the world, and the register for the room.

stages.title: Reading articles and literature
explain: French journalism often uses the passé composé for events, the imparfait for background, and the present for headlines. Passive structures and nominalisation (turning verbs into nouns) make the text dense: "Le gouvernement a annoncé une réforme" becomes "L'annonce d'une réforme".

In literature, Victor Hugo wrote "Les Misérables", Albert Camus wrote "L'Étranger", and Aimé Césaire from Martinique wrote about négritude. Reading strategy: find the topic sentence, identify connectors such as "cependant" and "en effet", and notice the tone.

gq.q: Why does a news article often use nominalisation?
o: It packs information into fewer words
gq.why: Turning verbs into nouns condenses text.

panel.q: What does "en effet" signal in a text?
o: Confirmation or explanation of the preceding idea

panel.q: Aimé Césaire is associated with which movement?
panel.why: Césaire co-founded négritude, which affirmed Black cultural identity.

panel.q: Why must a reader identify the narrator's point of view?
o: It shapes what is reliable or biased

points.ask: What do I notice in literature?

teach.model: In a French article, read the headline and lead first. Look for connectors like cependant and en effet. Notice tense: passé composé for events, imparfait for background. In literature, identify the narrator and tone.

stages.hook: How is a French newspaper article different from a short story?
stages.mnemonic: Headline, lead, details: read in that order.

stages.title: Essay and correspondence writing
explain: A formal letter opens with "Madame, Monsieur," and closes with a formula such as "Veuillez agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées." An informal letter opens with "Cher Paul," or "Chère Marie," and closes with "Amitiés" or "Bises".
An essay has an introduction, development and conclusion. Use connectors: "tout d'abord", "en outre", "par conséquent", "en revanche", "en conclusion". Avoid repeating words and keep sentences clear.
sentences: I am writing to ask for information.
On the other hand, prices are high.

gq.q: Which opening suits a formal letter to an unknown person?
gq.why: Madame, Monsieur is the standard formal opening.

gq.q: Why is the closing formula so long in French?
o: Politeness conventions are expected in formal writing
gq.why: Formal writing follows set courtesy formulas.

panel.q: Which connector introduces a contrast?
panel.why: En revanche means on the other hand.

panel.q: Which is the correct opening for a letter to a woman friend?
Why must an essay conclusion not add a new argument?
o: It should summarise and answer the question

points.ask: How do I open to a friend?
What do I use in essays?

teach.model: A formal French letter begins with Madame, Monsieur, states its purpose and ends with a long courtesy formula. Friends are addressed with Cher or Chère. An essay has introduction, development and conclusion linked by connectors.

stages.hook: How do you begin and end a formal letter in French, when you cannot write "Dear" or "Yours sincerely" directly?
stages.mnemonic: Formal letter: greeting, purpose, request, formula.

stages.title: Translation fundamentals
explain: Good translation preserves meaning, not word order. Translate "It's raining cats and dogs" as "Il pleut des cordes", not as "Il pleut des chats et des chiens." Beware of false friends: "actuellement" is not "actually" (which is "en fait").

Watch for structural differences. English adjectives come before the noun, French often after. English "I'm 20" becomes "J'ai vingt ans". The English "-ing" has no direct French equivalent: "I like swimming" becomes "J'aime nager". Choose between literal, free and idiomatic translation depending on purpose.

gq.q: Why is "Il pleut des chats et des chiens" a bad translation?
o: It translates words, not the idiom's meaning
gq.why: Idioms must be replaced by an equivalent expression.

panel.q: What does "actuellement" mean in a translation of "currently"?
How is "I like swimming" best translated?
panel.why: French uses an infinitive after aimer.

panel.q: Why do translators sometimes change sentence structure?
o: To sound natural in the target language

teach.model: Translate meaning, not word for word. Watch false friends such as actuellement and idioms such as il pleut des cordes. Notice structural differences: English -ing becomes an infinitive and age uses avoir.

stages.hook: What is the best translation of "It's raining cats and dogs" into French?

stages.title: Regional varieties and cultural context
explain: French is spoken on every inhabited continent. In Belgium and Switzerland, people say "septante" and "nonante" for 70 and 90, where France says "soixante-dix" and "quatre-vingt-dix". In Quebec, "le déjeuner" is breakfast and "le souper" is dinner, and "char" can mean car.

In West and Central Africa, French is an official language in many countries, such as Senegal, Côte d'Ivoire and Cameroon, and coexists with languages like Wolof and Bambara. The Organisation internationale de la Francophonie links French-speaking countries. Haiti has Haitian Creole alongside French.
sentences: In Quebec, people have breakfast early.

gq.q: What do Belgians and Swiss often say for 70?
Why does Quebec French keep some older forms?
o: It developed apart from France for centuries
gq.why: Isolation preserved old words and sounds.

panel.q: Why is "déjeuner" different in France and Quebec?
o: In France it is lunch; in Quebec it is breakfast

panel.q: What does the Francophonie represent?
panel.why: It is an international organisation and a cultural space.

panel.q: Why is it wrong to call one variety "correct French" and others "wrong"?
o: All varieties follow rules and have legitimate standards

teach.model: French has regional varieties. Belgium and Switzerland use septante and nonante. Quebec uses déjeuner, dîner and souper for breakfast, lunch and dinner. In many African countries French is official alongside local languages.

stages.hook: Do people in Quebec, Senegal, Belgium and Switzerland all speak the same French?
stages.mnemonic: One language, many voices: la Francophonie.

stages.title: Structured debates and presentations
explain: A good argument has a claim, reasons and an example. Introduce your position: "Je pense que...", "À mon avis...", "Je soutiens que...". Add: "En outre...". Respond: "Certes, mais...", "Je comprends votre point de vue, cependant...".
A presentation has an opening, three parts and a conclusion. Use a clear voice and signposts: "Tout d'abord", "Ensuite", "Pour conclure". End by thanking the audience: "Merci de votre attention."
items: je comprends votre point de vue
sentences: In my opinion, school should start later.
Admittedly, but the facts are different.

gq.q: Which phrase answers an opponent politely?
gq.why: Certes concedes a point before replying.

gq.q: Why does a speaker use signposts like "tout d'abord"?
o: They help listeners follow the structure

panel.q: Which verb form follows "Je pense que"?
panel.why: Je pense que (affirmative) takes the indicative.

panel.q: How does a speaker end a talk politely?
o: Pour conclure... Merci de votre attention
panel.why: It is a standard formal closing.

panel.q: Why include an example in an argument?
o: It makes a claim concrete and testable

points.ask: How do I state a position?
How do I structure a talk?

teach.model: State your position with à mon avis or je pense que. Support it with reasons and examples. Answer opponents with certes, mais. Use signposts like tout d'abord and pour conclure, and thank the audience.

stages.hook: How do you structure a short debate speech in French and respond to the other side?
stages.mnemonic: Claim, reason, example, then reply with "certes, mais".
